To jinx something or someone means to bring bad luck to it, or to cause something to go wrong, usually without meaning to. When you jinx something, you don't necessarily do anything physically harmful — the "damage" happens through superstition, fate, or bad luck that seems to follow.

Think of it this way: a jinx is like an invisible curse that you accidentally place on a person, a situation, or an event, making things go wrong when they were going well.

The word only makes sense if you understand the superstition it's built on: people believe that speaking too confidently about a good thing — or celebrating too early — can cause that good thing to fail.

It's the idea that luck is fragile. If you boast about it, announce it, or take it for granted, you might accidentally "break" it. This is irrational — most people know that — but the feeling is deeply human, which is why the word is used so widely.
The Two Main Ways "Jinx" Is Used as a Verb

1. To jinx someone or something by speaking too soon

This is the most common use. You jinx something when you say something confidently about a good outcome before it has actually happened, and then things go wrong.

"She said the surgery would go perfectly. She totally jinxed it — there were complications."

"Don't jinx it by saying we've already won. The game isn't over yet!"

Here, jinxing is caused by words — specifically by premature confidence or celebration. The person didn't do anything evil. They just spoke too soon, and bad luck followed (or so people believe).

2. To jinx someone simply by bringing bad luck around them

In a broader sense, you can jinx someone just by being near them or being involved with them in a way that seems to attract misfortune.

"Every team he plays for loses the championship. He jinxes every team he joins."

"I'm not inviting him to the launch. He jinxes everything."

Here, it's less about a specific statement and more about a pattern of bad luck that seems to follow a person.
The Most Famous Phrase: "Don't jinx it!"

You will hear this constantly in everyday English. It's what someone says when another person is being too optimistic or celebrating prematurely.

Friend A: "I'm definitely going to get that job. I can already feel it!"
Friend B: "Shhh! Don't jinx it!"

Friend B is warning Friend A: stop saying that out loud — you might cause it not to happen. It's a playful but genuine expression of superstitious caution.

Similarly, people say "You jinxed us!" to blame someone after something goes wrong, especially if that person was being overly confident beforehand.
Who Jinxes Whom? (The Grammar of It)

As a verb, "jinx" always needs a target — something or someone that is jinxed.

  • You jinx a person → "Stop talking like that, you're going to jinx me!"
  • You jinx an event → "He jinxed the wedding by predicting it would be flawless."
  • You jinx a team or group → "Don't put that banner up yet — you'll jinx the team."
  • You jinx a streak or situation → "She jinxed our winning streak."

"Jinx" is an informal, everyday word. You'd hear it in casual conversations, in sports commentary, among friends and family. It is not used in formal writing, legal language, or academic text.

It can be said playfully ("You jinxed it, you goofball!") or in genuine frustration ("I swear you jinxed this entire project."). The tone depends on the situation, but the word itself is never harsh or offensive.

It's important to separate "jinx" from similar-sounding ideas:

  • It is not a deliberate act of harm. Unlike a curse someone casts on purpose with malicious intent, jinxing is almost always accidental. Nobody means to jinx things — it just happens through careless optimism or bad luck.
  • It does not imply any supernatural power on the part of the person doing the jinxing. They aren't a witch or a villain. They're just someone who seems to attract misfortune.
  • It is not the same as a literal curse. Jinx is a casual, everyday word. Saying someone jinxed something is not a serious accusation — it's a light, often half-joking remark rooted in superstition.

To jinx something = to bring bad luck to it, usually by being too confident, celebrating too early, or simply being associated with misfortune. It is rooted in superstition, used in casual speech, and almost always describes something that happens by accident, not intent. The word is used both playfully and with genuine frustration, and it's one of the most common superstition-related words in everyday English.
